1.note: See how you translated the phrase “And it happened” in 2:39, where it similarly introduces a new event.

The author is describing the time between one year and another in the way that is characteristic of his culture. In your translation, express this the way a speaker of your language naturally would. Alternate translation: [in the 480th year]
See the discussion of this phrase in the introduction to 1 Kings. Alternate translation: [the Israelite people]

1.q: בַּ⁠שָּׁנָ֨ה הָ⁠רְבִיעִ֜ית בְּ⁠חֹ֣דֶשׁ זִ֗ו ה֚וּא הַ⁠חֹ֣דֶשׁ הַ⁠שֵּׁנִ֔י לִ⁠מְלֹ֥ךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֖ה עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל
1.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **the fourth year** and the information about **the reigning of Solomon** together. Alternate translation: [in the fourth year of the reigning of Solomon over Israel, in the month of Ziv (it is the second month)]

The author is providing background information to help readers recognize that **Ziv** was the official name at this time for the month that they knew simply as **the second month**. In your translation, present this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The **second month** of the Hebrew calendar, which the author identifies as the **month of Ziv**, includes the months of April and May on Western calendars. You could convert the Hebrew month into approximate dates on the calendar that your culture uses. However, the Jews used a lunar calendar, so if you use a solar calendar, the dates will be different every year, and the translation will not be entirely accurate. So you may just want to give the name of the month on the Hebrew calendar and say in a footnote approximately what time of year that is on your calendar.

Be sure that it is clear in your translation that this was the **second month** of the agricultural year, not the **second month** of Solomon’s **fourth year** of **reigning**. Alternate translation: [it is the second month of the year]
See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of the term “second.” Alternate translation: [month two]

Since the author says in 6:38 that Solomon “built” the temple over the course of “seven years,” he does not mean here that Solomon **built the house of Yahweh** entirely **in the fourth year** of his reign. Your language may have a verb form or verbal phrase that you can use in your translation that indicates the beginning of an action. Alternate translation: [that he began to build]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:26. Alternate translation: [that Solomon had his workers build] or [that Solomon commanded his workers to begin to build]
See how you translated the similar expression in [3:1](ta:03). Alternate translation: [the temple of Yahweh]

2.note: See the discussion of the term “cubits” in the introduction to this chapter for suggestions as to how you might represent the lengths that the author is using the term to indicate.

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and 20 cubits]

3.q: עַל־פְּנֵי֙ הֵיכַ֣ל הַ⁠בַּ֔יִת & עַל־פְּנֵ֖י רֹ֣חַב הַ⁠בָּ֑יִת & עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הַ⁠בָּֽיִת
3.note: In each of these instances, the phrase **on the face of** represents being in front of something. The author is using the phrase in three slightly different ways. In the first instance, he means that the **porch** was in front of the **nave of the house**. That is, priests would walk across the porch to enter the main hall of the temple. In the second instance, he means that the porch was in front of the entire **width of the house**. That is, its length of**20 cubits** corresponded to the width of the **house** or temple. In the third instance, the author means that the porch extended out **Ten** cubits in front of the temple. If it would be helpful in your language, in your translation you could use equivalent expressions or plain language. Alternate translation: [that was in front of the nave of the house … corresponding to the width of the house … extending outward from the house]

While, in other contexts, the term translated as **nave** can mean “palace” or “temple,” the author is using it in a specialized sense here. He is referring to a specific architectural feature of Solomon’s temple, the main hall that was the equivalent of the Holy Place in the sacred tent. If your culture has a term for such a feature, you could use that in your translation, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the main hall]

See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of how the author uses the phrase **Ten by the cubit** to express a distance in a way characteristic of his culture. Alternate translation: [Ten cubits]

4.note: By **windows with narrowed frames**, the author means windows with narrowed or beveled frames that were wider on the inside of the wall than on the outside. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [windows that were narrower on the outside than on the inside] or [windows with frames that widened toward the inside]

5.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [that is, against the walls of the house all around, both the wall of the nave and the wall of the inner sanctuary]

The author is clarifying that the **addition** that Solomon had his workers build extended all the way around the sides and back of the temple building. If he had simply said **the wall of the house**, some readers might have understood this not to include the back third of the temple, which consisted of the Most Holy Place. So he adds that the addition rested against the **walls** of both the **nave** and the **inner sanctuary**. Readers in some cultures might consider these to be the same wall, and so it may be more natural for you to express this in your translation by using a singular form. Alternate translation: [extending around the outer wall of both the nave and the inner sanctuary]

Here the author is using a technical architectural term that occurs only in the descriptions of Solomon’s temple here in 1 Kings, in the parallel passages in 2 Chronicles, and in Psalm 28:2. He means the innermost part of the temple, which corresponded to the Holy of Holies or Most Holy Place in the sacred tent. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use one of those names, as the UST does, or you could use a general expression. Alternate translation: [the innermost part of the temple]

6.note: While the author is using the same word here that is translated as **addition** in the previous verse, here he is using a feminine form to mean one part of the structure, specifically one of its three floors. In the previous verse and in 6:10, the author uses the masculine form to mean the entire structure. If your language uses forms of different gender in the same way, you could do that here in your translation. If not, you could indicate the meaning explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The lowest floor of the addition]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the middle floor … and the third floor]

The term **third** refers here to the highest of the three levels of rooms built alongside the temple walls, as mentioned in verse 5 and in verse 8. If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **third**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [and floor three] or [and the highest floor]
Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Alternate translation: [This was possible because]

7.note: The expressions **in its being built** and **was built** are passive verbal forms. If your language would not use these forms, you could express the idea with active forms or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [When the workers built the temple, they built it]

The expression **was not heard** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [So no one heard hammers or the chisel, any implement of iron]

The author is not referring to a specific **chisel**. He means **any** chisel or any similar **implement of iron** that would have made a loud sound when it struck **stone**. Since this is his meaning, it may also be more natural to use a singular form of “hammer” instead of the plural form **hammers**. Alternate translation: [So no hammer or chisel, no implement of iron, was heard]

The expression **in its being built** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [in the temple while the workers were building it]

8.note: The author is not referring to a specific **middle chamber**. He means the rooms on the middle level in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the middle chambers] or [the second floor]

The author is using the term **shoulder** to mean the side of the **house** or temple. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [was on the side of the temple at the right, near the front]

The author is speaking of directions in the way characteristic of his culture. He does not mean that if someone were standing in front of the temple, facing the porch, that this entrance would be on that person’s **right**. Instead, people of this culture spoke of directions as if a person were facing east, toward the sunrise. The south would be to the right of such a person. So the author means that this entrance was on the south side of the temple. (It was actually on the left of a person who was standing in front of the temple, facing the porch.) Alternate translation: [was on the south side of the temple, near the front]

Here the author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific individuals. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people went up] or [and the priests went up]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [onto the middle floor, and they also went up by stairs from the middle floor to the third floor]

9.note: Together, the verbs **built** and **finished** express a single idea. The word **finished** tells to what degree Solomon **built** the temple, that is, to completion. (The author is referring specifically to the walls of the temple.) If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way, here and in 6:14. Alternate translation: [And he finished building the house]

The author is probably using the plural form **cedars** because these **beams** and **boards** came from many different cedar trees. It may be more natural in some languages to use a singular form to indicate the composition of these beams and boards, here and in the next verse. Alternate translation: [of cedar]

10.q: וַ⁠יִּ֤בֶן אֶת־ה⁠יצוע עַל־כָּל־הַ⁠בַּ֔יִת חָמֵ֥שׁ אַמּ֖וֹת קֽוֹמָת֑⁠וֹ וַ⁠יֶּאֱחֹ֥ז אֶת־הַ⁠בַּ֖יִת בַּ⁠עֲצֵ֥י אֲרָזִֽים
10.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about how the addition **held {onto}** to the temple with the information that Solomon built it **against** or right next to the temple. Alternate translation: [And he built the addition against all of the house, and it held onto the house with wood of cedars. Five cubits was its height]

The author is saying **all of the house** as a generalization for emphasis. The context makes clear that no part of the addition was in front of the temple, where there was a porch. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [all around the sides and back of the temple]

The author expects readers to understand that each of the three levels of rooms was five cubits high. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [five cubits was the height of each of its levels]

11.note: The author is using a common expression of his culture to mean that Yahweh spoke a message to Solomon. If this expression does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 2 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 2 Samuel 7:4. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh spoke a message to Solomon]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:5.

12.q: הַ⁠בַּ֨יִת הַ⁠זֶּ֜ה אֲשֶׁר־אַתָּ֣ה בֹנֶ֗ה אִם־תֵּלֵ֤ךְ בְּ⁠חֻקֹּתַ⁠י֙ וְ⁠אֶת־מִשְׁפָּטַ֣⁠י תַּֽעֲשֶׂ֔ה וְ⁠שָׁמַרְתָּ֥ אֶת־כָּל־מִצְוֺתַ֖⁠י לָ⁠לֶ֣כֶת בָּ⁠הֶ֑ם וַ⁠הֲקִמֹתִ֤י אֶת־דְּבָרִ⁠י֙ אִתָּ֔⁠ךְ אֲשֶׁ֥ר דִּבַּ֖רְתִּי אֶל־דָּוִ֥ד אָבִֽי⁠ךָ׃ וְ⁠שָׁ֣כַנְתִּ֔י בְּ⁠ת֖וֹךְ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְ⁠לֹ֥א אֶעֱזֹ֖ב אֶת־עַמִּ֥⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
12.note: If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine 6:12 and 6:13 into a verse bridge in order to put the information together that Yahweh would “dwell” in the **house** or temple that Solomon was **building**.

See how you translated the similar expression in 3:14. You may have chosen to indicate that the image of walking represents living, and you may have chosen to express the meaning of the similar terms “statutes” and “commandments” with a single term. (You can include the further term that occurs here, **judgments**, in such a single term.) Alternate translation: [if, by obeying all of my laws, you live as I want people to live]

It might seem that saying **if you walk … by walking in them** would be to express extra information in a way that would not be natural in your language. If so, if you choose to retain the image of walking in your translation, you could choose to express it only once. Alternate translation: [if you walk in all of my laws]

12.q: וַ⁠הֲקִמֹתִ֤י אֶת־דְּבָרִ⁠י֙ אִתָּ֔⁠ךְ אֲשֶׁ֥ר דִּבַּ֖רְתִּי אֶל
12.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 2:4. Alternate translation: [then I will make happen for you what I said when I spoke with]

14.note: The author interrupted his account of the construction of the temple in 6:11–13 to report what Yahweh told Solomon. He is now resuming that account where he left off at 6:10, with the outer walls and roof in place but nothing on the interior of the walls. Use a word, phrase, or other method here that is natural in your language for reminding readers where a story has left off. If you have already translated the book of 1 Samuel, see what you did in the similar case of 1 Samuel 29:1, where the biblical author similarly resumes a story after an interruption. Alternate translation: [Now Solomon’s workers had finished building the temple walls and roof]

15.note: The author is using the possessive form to describe the part of the **walls** that were near the **ceiling**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the part of the walls near the ceiling] or [the top of the walls]

16.note: By saying that Solomon **built 20 cubits**, the author means that he built a structure that extended out 20 cubits from the back wall of the temple. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [a structure 20 cubits deep]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the part of the walls near the ceiling] or [the top of the walls]

The pronoun **them** refers to the 20 cubits that the author speaks of earlier in this verse, meaning a structure 20 cubits deep. The pronoun **it** refers to the **house** or temple. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And he built that area 20 cubits deep for the temple]

17.note: As the author indicates, by **the house** he means **the nave**, that is, the rest of the temple, the main room in front of the inner sanctuary. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the rest of the temple]

Here, **to the face of it** represents being in front of the inner sanctuary. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of it]

18.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [it was decorated with carving of gourds and opened ones of flowers]

The author is not referring to a specific **carving**. He means carvings in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [carvings of gourds]

The expression **opened ones** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language, here and in verses 29 and 35. Alternate translation: [and flowers that had opened]

The expression **was seen** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no one saw any stone]

21.note: Since the author has already described in the previous verse how Solomon overlaid the inner sanctuary with gold, here the term **house** probably refers to the rest of the temple, that is, the nave or main hall. Alternate translation: [the interior walls of the rest of the temple]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of the inner sanctuary. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of]

The pronoun **it** probably refers to the exterior wall of the inner sanctuary, which faced the main hall. The author described in the previous verse how all of its interior walls were overlaid with gold. Here he is describing how its one exterior wall was also overlaid. Alternate translation: [and he overlaid the outside wall of the inner sanctuary]

22.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition. The author is using a poetic form to provide a summary statement of the entire process of overlaying the temple interior with gold. It would be good to show this to your readers by representing both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. There may be a natural way to do this in your language. Alternate translation: [So he overlaid the temple interior with gold until there was no part of it that was not overlaid with gold]
This could mean: (1) Alternate translation: [that was in front of the inner sanctuary] or (2) Alternate translation: [that was associated with the inner sanctuary]

23.note: The author is using the possessive form to describe **wood** that comes from a tree whose fruit produces **oil**. In other words, he means wood from an olive tree, or olive wood. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way, here and in verses 31, 32, and 33. Alternate translation: [olive wood]

Here the author is beginning to describe one of the cherubs. He describes its height in this sentence and its wingspan in the next verse. In the following two verses, he then describes the wingspan and height of the other cherub. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine 6:23–26 into a verse bridge in order to describe both cherubs together rather than each one separately.

24.q: עֶ֣שֶׂר אַמּ֔וֹת מִ⁠קְצ֥וֹת כְּנָפָ֖י⁠ו וְ⁠עַד־קְצ֥וֹת כְּנָפָֽי⁠ו
24.note: This second sentence in the verse means basically the same thing as the first one. However, it is not redundant or unnecessary. The author is building up to his statement in 6:27 that the wings of the cherubs stretched across the entire 20-cubit width of the Holy of Holies. The movement from **five** to **ten** to an implied twenty creates a sense of majesty around these cherubs, which represented the presence of Yahweh in his temple. It would be good to give your readers the experience the author intended by including this sentence separately in your translation rather than combining it with the first sentence in some way.

24.q: עֶ֣שֶׂר אַמּ֔וֹת מִ⁠קְצ֥וֹת כְּנָפָ֖י⁠ו וְ⁠עַד־קְצ֥וֹת כְּנָפָֽי⁠ו
24.note: The author is describing the distance from one extreme to another in the way that was characteristic of his culture. He uses the plural form **ends** where other languages might use a singular form. In your translation, express this the way people of your culture would describe the distance between two extremes. Alternate translation: [It was ten cubits from one end of its wings to the other]

25.note: Since the author describes the second cherub’s height in the next verse, he seems to be describing the second cherub’s wingspan here. Alternate translation: [was the wingspan of the second cherub]

27.note: Here the author uses the expression **the inner house** to mean the same part of the temple that he calls “the inner sanctuary” in the rest of this chapter. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the inner sanctuary]

Here the author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. He is putting the focus on the way the wings of the cherubs **spread out** across the whole width of the Holy of Holies, not on who put them in this position. Use an expression to convey this meaning that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the wings of the cherubs were spread out] or [And the wings of the cherubs extended outward]

29.note: The workers first carved these designs into the walls, and then they overlaid the walls with gold. (The author describes this sequence explicitly in 6:32 in the case of the doors.) See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of why the author describes the carvings and overlay of the two parts of the temple in the order that he does. Your language may have a verb form or verb phrase that you can use in your translation to indicate that the action in this verse preceded the action in 6:22. Alternate translation: [he had carved]

The author is using a possessive form to describe **carvings** that were **engravings**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [engraved carvings]

The author is using the adjectives **inside** and **outside** as nouns to mean certain parts of the temple. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases here and in the next verse. Alternate translation: [from the inside room and to the outside room] or [in both the inner sanctuary and the main hall]

31.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [The length of the lintel and the height of the doorposts were each one fifth of the 20-cubit length and height of the inner sanctuary wall]
A **fifth** means one part out of five equal parts.

32.note: The context indicates that the workers also **beat out** the **gold** that they had **overlaid** on the **flowers**. You can include the flowers in this statement if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [on the cherubs, the palm trees, and the flowers]

33.note: The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [from a fourth of the width of the wall] or [one fourth as wide as the wall]
A **fourth** means one part out of four equal parts.

34.note: Some ancient manuscripts read “curtains.” The ULT follows that reading. One ancient manuscript and several ancient versions read “leaves.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

35.note: The expression **smoothed onto the carved things** uses a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [which the workers smoothed onto the carvings]

36.note: The expression **inner courtyard** represents a wall that Solomon’s workers built in order to create a courtyard around the temple. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the wall of the inner courtyard]

37.q: בַּ⁠שָּׁנָה֙ הָֽ⁠רְבִיעִ֔ית יֻסַּ֖ד בֵּ֣ית יְהוָ֑ה בְּ⁠יֶ֖רַח זִֽו
37.note: In this verse and the next one, the author is concluding his account of how Solomon had his workers build a temple for Yahweh. Here he repeats what he said at the beginning of the account, in [6:1](ta:06), about when Solomon began the project. That repetition signals the impending conclusion of the account, which ends in the next verse with the author’s statement of when Solomon completed the project. Use a natural form in your language for concluding an account with a brief summary of what it has described.

37.q: בַּ⁠שָּׁנָה֙ הָֽ⁠רְבִיעִ֔ית יֻסַּ֖ד בֵּ֣ית יְהוָ֑ה בְּ⁠יֶ֖רַח זִֽו
37.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the **month** of Ziv with the information about the **year**. Alternate translation: [In the fourth year, in the month of Ziv, the house of Yahweh was founded]

By **the fourth year**, the author means the fourth year of Solomon’s reign as king. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [In the fourth year of the reign of Solomon]
If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **fourth**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [In year four]

The expression **was founded** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [workers laid the foundation of the house of Yahweh]

38.note: If your language would not use a form such as **year 11**, you could describe this year with a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [And in the eleventh year]
See how you translated the similar expression in [6:1](ta:06), where the author was also explaining that a month he describes by a name was one that his readers likely knew by a number.
See how you decided to represent a Hebrew month in [6:1](ta:06).

The author is speaking of the **house** as if it had been a living thing that could have **finished** its own construction. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the workers finished building the temple]

The pronoun translated as **its** could also mean “his.” The author could be saying that: (1) by the date he names, the workers had completed every part of the temple according to the design they were working from. Alternate translation: [in every single part, just as designed] or (2) that the workers had done what Solomon had told and required them to do. Alternate translation: [according to all of his words and all of his requirements] or [just as Solomon had said and required it should be]
